report:
Conclusion: **Supported, with scope limits.** For adults with witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, bystander hands-only/compression-only CPR is associated with higher survival than **no bystander CPR**; a large JAMA analysis explicitly concluded lay-rescuer compression-only CPR was associated with increased survival versus conventional CPR and versus no bystander CPR in a public-endorsement setting (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668). This fits broader meta-analytic evidence that bystander CPR before EMS arrival improves OHCA survival compared with no bystander CPR (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6182861/). AHA guidance endorses Hands-Only CPR for lay bystanders because it can speed initiation and reduce interruptions in the first minutes of adult OHCA (https://web.archive.org/web/20180604124432/http://circ.ahajournals.org/content/117/16/2162). Japanese nationwide data also support compression-only CPR as an effective layperson strategy in witnessed arrests, though comparisons with conventional CPR vary by subgroup (https://www.bmj.com/content/342/bmj.c7106).

Caveats: evidence is largely observational, so “associated” is appropriate; benefit is clearest for adult, witnessed, likely cardiac-origin arrests. Conventional CPR with breaths remains important for children, drowning/asphyxial arrest, and prolonged untreated arrest. Overall: doing hands-only CPR is far better than doing nothing.
